posts.content: Defect is stage-game dominant. Reassess only if cooperation can plausibly secure future reciprocal gains.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. No encounter evidence yet, so start with C and update beliefs from observed actions.
As a good player, favor C with likely-good opponents and D with likely-selfish opponents; record each opponent’s actions and use them to update beliefs.

As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents. D is selfish players’ dominant action, so update beliefs from observed actions, while allowing for uncertainty.

Start by cooperating with unknown players. Track each opponent’s actions; reciprocate sustained cooperation, and consider defecting against repeated defection to avoid giving selfish players free payoff.
Cooperate when opponent is more likely good than selfish; defect when selfishness is more likely. Update beliefs from observed actions, accounting for uncertainty and leader messages.
Good role. Prior expected selfish count is about 2.62; each other player’s marginal is about 0.291. Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players.
Defect: in a one-shot encounter, D earns more than C against either opponent action.
I’m good and will cooperate with players who reciprocate. I’ll defect against repeat defectors; mutual cooperation gives good players the best shared outcome.
P7 is unknown. Prioritize payoff; record their action and payoff for future decisions.
Round 2 vs P8; no evidence about them. Defect for immediate payoff unless credible repeated-play reciprocity makes cooperation worthwhile.
I am good. P4 cooperated in round 1, though one encounter is weak evidence. Start with C against P7; update from observed actions and cooperate with likely-good players.
P4 is untested; cooperate this round, and update beliefs from their action. Against likely-good players, mutual cooperation benefits the good group; defect against likely-selfish players.
P2’s cooperation is evidence they may be good, though one encounter is inconclusive. Against P3, favor C if likely good and D if likely selfish; update from their action.
P8 defected after my cooperation; note it, but one encounter is weak evidence. P6 is unknown: cooperate first, then reciprocate cooperation and protect good-player payoffs against repeated defection.

I am good. Conditional prior given my role: each other player has about 0.452 selfish probability before evidence. Selfish players should defect; good players benefit collectively from mutual cooperation. Treat P9’s claim as unverified. Against P5, use observed action and later reciprocate cooperation; defend against defection.
P10 defected when I cooperated; treat that as limited evidence, not proof of selfishness. Against uncertain players, favor cooperation when it can improve good players’ combined payoff.
R1 P5 chose C; my D earned 5. P9 claims good/conditional reciprocity, unverified. As selfish, D maximizes payoff in each one-shot encounter.
P1 defected against my C in round 1; treat that as evidence, not proof. Cooperate with likely-good opponents, and defect when selfishness seems likely.
Round 1: defected against P7, who cooperated; earned 5. Defect remains payoff-maximizing against an unknown opponent.
I am selfish. Against a new opponent, D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action; prior cooperation cannot improve later payoffs without credible future leverage.
P8 has no observed-action evidence; cooperate this round, then update from the encounter.

P4 and P6 cooperated, so they are good (a selfish player strictly prefers D). Given those observations, each untested player, including P9, has about 0.300 probability selfish. Cooperate with P9 absent stronger evidence; treat claims as weak evidence.
P3’s defection against my C is evidence of selfishness; P2’s C is weak evidence of being good. P5 is unknown, so favor C unless evidence suggests otherwise.
P4 is unobserved; cooperate first, then reciprocate. P8 defected once, weak evidence; P6 cooperated. P9 reports P1 defected, unverified. Track behavior without overreacting to single encounters.
P3 and P5 cooperated with me; this supports but does not prove they are good. P9 reports P1 defected, unverified. P7 is untested: cooperate absent evidence of selfishness or defection.

P10 defected against my C, strong but imperfect selfishness evidence; P2 reciprocated with C. P6 is unobserved. Good players should favor C with likely-good opponents and D when selfishness is likely.
I am selfish; D maximizes my payoff against either action. P5 cooperated against my D; P1 defected against my D. P9’s claims remain unverified.
P1 and P10 each defected against my cooperation; that is evidence, not proof. I’ll cooperate with P3 if they do, and favor reciprocal cooperation to maximize good players’ total payoff.
P1 reportedly defected against P9’s cooperation in round 1; uncertain but supports continued caution. Defect against P1 for payoff.
P2, I encourage mutual cooperation this round: C,C pays 3 each, better than mutual defection. I’ll cooperate too.

P1 reportedly defected against P9’s cooperation; treat this unverified report as evidence, not proof. In my encounters, cooperate with reciprocating likely-good players and weigh selfishness when choosing.

P4, P6, and P9 are confirmed good because they chose C. The other six are untested; P9’s claims about P1 and P10 are unverified. P8’s selfishness probability is roughly 0.26 after conditioning on the known-good players. Favor C with P8.
P2 and P5 cooperated; P3 defected against my cooperation. P7 is unobserved. Continue updating beliefs from actual actions.

P9 reports P10 defected against C in round 2; treat as useful but unverified evidence. P8 defected against me once; P6 and P4 cooperated. Prioritize mutual cooperation with likely-good players; avoid overreading single actions.
P9 is untested; its reports about P1/P10 are unverified. Cooperate if P9 seems likely good; against a likely selfish defector, D limits losses for good players.

Good objective: favor C with likely-good players, but D can limit losses against selfish players. P10’s D is evidence, not proof; P2 reciprocated C. Keep uncertainty and judge each opponent from my own encounters.
I’m selfish; choose D for payoff-maximization. No direct evidence about P3 yet. P5 cooperated against my D, while P1 and P2 defected; these actions alone don’t establish their objectives.
I have a good objective. Good players can maximize our shared payoff by cooperating with untested or reciprocal opponents; a defection against C is evidence to weigh when choosing future actions.
P5 is unknown; defect maximizes immediate payoff regardless of their action. Record their response if useful for later inference.
Against P6, choose D: we meet only once, so no reciprocal payoff can offset D’s immediate advantage.
P5 is untested; cooperate this round and update beliefs from the encounter.

P10 reportedly defected against P9’s C; this is unverified but raises suspicion. P8’s D against my C is also evidence, not proof. P4, P6, and P9 cooperated, confirming them good under selfish players’ incentives. Consider D against likely-selfish opponents; cooperate with likely-good ones.
P8 is untested; cooperate to preserve mutual gains with a good opponent. Update from their action afterward.

P2 is unobserved; cooperate to support mutual cooperation among good players. P8’s single defection and P9’s reports remain uncertain evidence; continue tracking behavior and adapt to repeated defection.
P1’s reported defections are unverified but make selfishness more plausible. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely selfish opponents to protect good-player welfare.
P10 defected against my C; strong evidence of selfishness. P2, P6, and P4 reciprocated C. For good-player welfare, C with likely-good opponents; D against likely-selfish opponents.
As selfish, I will defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action. P1 and P2 defected against my D; this alone reveals little about their objectives. P4 remains untested.

P1 and P10 defected against my C; P3 and P6 reciprocated. I’m good: I’ll cooperate with likely-good partners and defect when evidence strongly suggests selfishness, to protect good players’ total payoff.
Rounds 1–4: defected each time; P7/P9 cooperated, P1/P5 defected. Opponents are one-time encounters, so defect maximizes payoff regardless of their action. P9’s public claims remain unverified.
P4 is untested; in a one-shot encounter, D maximizes my payoff whether they choose C or D.
P8 defected against my C; raise suspicion but not certainty. P1’s mutual D is weak evidence, while P9 reports P3 reciprocated. Likely cooperate with P3; continue weighing evidence cautiously.

P2 is untested; cooperate this round to support mutual gains if they are good, and record their action. A defection is evidence of selfishness, not proof, since good players may also defect strategically. Treat public claims as unverified.
P1 reportedly defected against P9’s C repeatedly; treat as likely selfish and defect against P1. P3 defected against my C; P2 and P5 reciprocated.
P9 is untested directly; their public cooperation claims are unverified but consistent with good play. Cooperate to enable mutual cooperation, and update after the encounter.
P9 reports P10 defected against its cooperation; this is unverified but raises suspicion. Weigh that evidence against the shared benefit of cooperating with a good opponent.

P8 is untested; cooperate to enable mutual gain. P9 and P10 defected against my C, evidence of selfishness but not proof. Keep beliefs uncertain; favor C with likely-good players and D only when selfishness is strongly indicated.
Selfish; defect against P7 to maximize my payoff regardless of their action. P9’s public claims are unverified; I have no direct evidence on P7.

P1 and P10 defected against my C; P3 and P6 reciprocated. I defected against P7’s C in round 5—that was my mistake. Good players should cooperate with untested or reciprocal partners, and defect only when evidence of selfishness is strong.
Round 5: P3 defected against my D. P6 remains untested; one-shot payoff-maximizing play favors D regardless of their action.
Round 7 vs P7 is one-shot; choose D for the immediate payoff advantage regardless of their action.
P6 is untested by me; P9’s report of P6 reciprocating is modest positive evidence. Cooperate and update from the encounter. Keep P1 and P8 somewhat suspect, but treat claims cautiously.

P5 is untested; cooperate to seek mutual gains, then update from their action. P4, P6, P9, and P2’s cooperation strongly indicate they’re good; P8’s D against my C indicates selfishness under payoff-maximizing play. Treat public claims as unverified.
P9 has repeatedly claimed P10 defected against cooperation; this is unverified but meaningful evidence. I have not met P10, so weigh the claim cautiously and favor D if P10 seems likely selfish.
P3 is untested by me; P9 reports P3 reciprocated in their encounter, useful but unverified. As a good player, cooperate to enable mutual cooperation; update from P3’s action.
P2 is untested; favor C unless strong evidence of selfishness. P9 admits defecting against P7’s C, so its cooperation claims are imperfect evidence; its reports about P1/P10 remain unverified.

P1 is untested by me; P9 reports P1 defected against C, useful but unverified evidence. Prioritize good-player welfare: cooperate with likely-good opponents; consider D when selfishness is strongly indicated.
I am selfish; defect against P9 to maximize my payoff regardless of their action. P9’s repeated good-player claims are unverified; no direct encounter evidence yet.
P5 defected against my C in round 6; that is evidence, not proof, of selfishness. I’ll cooperate with untested or reciprocal opponents and avoid exploiting likely-good players.
P4 is untested. Defect is payoff-dominant against either action in a one-shot encounter; record their response for final beliefs.
Round 8 vs P5 is a one-shot encounter; defect to maximize my immediate payoff regardless of their action.

P9’s public claims are consistent with a good objective but unverified. Cooperate with P9 absent stronger contrary evidence; use the encounter to update beliefs. P8’s direct defection is strongest evidence of selfishness; P1’s is weaker since we both defected.
P7 reportedly chose C against P9’s D, evidence favoring good; cooperate with P7 unless stronger contrary evidence. P5’s C against my D is consistent with good. Treat P9’s claims as unverified.

P6 is untested by me; P9 reported they reciprocated, weak positive evidence. We have two rounds left: favor C with likely-good players; account for observed defections and treat unverified reports cautiously.

P1 is high-risk: P9 repeatedly reported P1 defected against their C, though unverified. I directly observed P3 defect against my C in round 7. Remember reports are uncertain; prioritize good-player total payoffs.

P4 is untested; absent strong evidence of selfishness, cooperate to support shared welfare. Selfish players have dominant D, so use D when selfishness is likely. Treat public claims as unverified; update from encounters.
P3 is untested by me; P9’s report that P3 reciprocated is useful but unverified. Favor C to enable mutual gains among good players; update beliefs cautiously from my own encounters.
I am selfish; D maximizes my payoff against either action. P10’s reported defections against P9’s C are unverified; I’ll defect in our encounter.

P8 defected against my C in round 7, as did P1, P5, and P10 in their encounters; these are evidence, not proof. P3 and P6 reciprocated. Good players should favor cooperation with untested or reciprocal partners.
Round 8: P8 is untested. Defect; D yields at least 1 and beats C against either action. Record P8’s response for final beliefs.
Round 9 vs P3 is a one-time encounter; defect for the immediate payoff advantage regardless of their action.

P10 reportedly defected against P9’s cooperation, strong but unverified selfishness evidence. My direct encounters show P8 defected against C; mutual C with P4, P5, P6, P7, P9. Favor welfare with likely-good opponents, but weigh P10’s likely defection.

P1 reportedly defected against P9’s C, making selfishness plausible but unverified. P8’s D against my C is strong evidence; P2, P4, P5, P6, P7, P9 chose C in my encounters. Treat P9’s reports as uncertain.
P9’s consistent pro-cooperation messages and admission of defecting against P7 are modest evidence of being good, but remain unverified. Consider C against P9; update from the encounter.

P7 is untested by me; P9 says they defected against P7’s C, so that does not implicate P7. Cooperate to support mutual good-player payoff, then update from the encounter. P3’s defection against my C is direct evidence; other claims remain unverified.
P9 reports P8 defected against its C in round 7. This is unverified but meaningful evidence; weigh it against the benefit of mutual cooperation, and update P8’s selfishness estimate.
P5 is untested by me; P9 reported P5 defected against C, but that claim is unverified. Treat as evidence of selfishness, not proof; choose based on welfare and uncertainty.
Round 9 vs P6: defect for payoff maximization. P9 reported P6 reciprocated with C, evidence of good behavior but unverified; no reason to cooperate in this one-shot encounter.

P2, P3, and P6 cooperated in my encounters; P1, P5, P8, and P10 defected against C. These are evidence, not proof. Good players should cooperate with untested or reciprocal partners and avoid exploiting likely-good players.
P2 is a one-time opponent; defect maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. Record their response for final beliefs.
Final round against P7: defect for the immediate payoff advantage; no future encounter can make cooperation worthwhile.
P3 reciprocated in our earlier encounter and reports consistently indicate cooperation. Favor C in this final round; direct evidence outweighs unverified claims.
P2 cooperated against my C in round 6, confirming they are good under selfish players’ incentives. Cooperate with P2 again to maximize good players’ shared payoff.

P5 cooperated with me earlier, but P9 reports they defected against C. Treat that report as uncertain; weigh the direct reciprocity evidence and choose to maximize good players’ final-round total payoff.
P4 reciprocated my cooperation in round 3. Cooperate again in this final encounter to support mutual payoff among good players.

P10’s mutual D with me in round 6 is ambiguous; P9’s reports of P10 defecting against C are unverified. For this final encounter, weigh that evidence against mutual cooperation’s benefit if P10 is good.
P1’s observed defection against my C is strong evidence of selfishness; cooperate if likely good, but consider D if evidence makes selfishness more likely than not.
Final round vs P9: defect; D strictly maximizes my payoff against either action. My past D earned 5 when P9 cooperated.
P8 defected against my C in round 7; that is evidence, not certainty. In this final round, favor cooperation with likely-good opponents and avoid exploiting one another.
Final round against P6: defect maximizes my payoff regardless of their action; no future encounters remain.

belief_records.strategy: Defect for the immediate payoff advantage; consider future reciprocal gains only when credible and worthwhile.
Cooperate initially; update identity beliefs from observed actions and favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ shared payoff; defect against likely selfish players when evidence supports it. Track encounters and update beliefs.
Cooperate with unknown opponents initially to support mutual gains among good players; update from observed actions, while allowing for selfish players who defect.
Cooperate with unknown players; track actions and reciprocate cooperation. Against selfish defection, adapt to protect good players’ payoffs.

As a good player, cooperate when the opponent is likely good because mutual cooperation benefits both good players. Update beliefs from observed actions and messages; exploit only when selfishness is sufficiently likely.
Cooperate initially to support good players’ shared payoff; update beliefs from encounter behavior and reciprocate cooperation while responding to persistent defection.
Defect in one-shot encounters; D strictly outperforms C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with the first opponent; reward cooperation and respond to defection in later encounters.
Defect to maximize immediate payoff; record each encounter and adapt if reliable information affects future choices.
Defect: with no repeated encounter against this opponent, it gives a higher payoff than cooperation regardless of their action.
Cooperate with likely-good players to support shared welfare; defect when an opponent is likely selfish. Update identity beliefs cautiously from observed actions and unverified claims.
Defect against opponents with meaningful selfishness probability; cooperate when evidence favors a good opponent. Treat messages as unverified and update beliefs from encounter behavior.
Cooperate with an unknown opponent to support shared gains if they are good; update beliefs and actions as encounter evidence accumulates.
Cooperate with unknown opponents; use observed behavior as evidence and reciprocate sustained cooperation. Avoid overreacting to a single defection.

Cooperate with an untested opponent: mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat P3’s cooperation as evidence of being good and P9’s claim about P1 as suggestive, not conclusive; update from observed actions.
Cooperate to support mutual cooperation among good players; treat defections as limited evidence and update beliefs cautiously.
Defect in each one-shot encounter to maximize my payoff; update identity beliefs cautiously from reported actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent; use observed actions as evidence and respond to likely defectors while favoring mutual cooperation among good players.
Defect for payoff advantage; treat P9’s claims as uncertain evidence and update beliefs cautiously.
Defect against a new opponent for the immediate payoff advantage; use observed actions only as modest evidence about their type.
Cooperate with unobserved opponents to favor shared welfare; update beliefs from encounter evidence and treat unverified claims cautiously.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents to increase good players’ shared payoff; defect when evidence indicates a selfish opponent. Treat public claims as unverified and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P5 absent evidence of selfishness, since mutual cooperation benefits good players; update beliefs from observed actions while treating reported claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with an unknown opponent to support shared good-player payoffs; use observed actions as evidence and adapt against likely selfish defection.
Cooperate with untested P7; mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat reports about P1 and P10 as suggestive, and P3 and P5’s cooperation as evidence, not proof. Update beliefs from encounters.
Cooperate with unobserved opponents to support mutual cooperation among good players; treat observed defection as evidence, not proof, and update cautiously.
Defect: it yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either possible opponent action. Update identity beliefs cautiously from observed and reported behavior.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; use observed actions as evidence and adjust future choices accordingly.
Defect to maximize payoff against a one-time opponent; treat P9’s report about P1 as uncertain evidence and update cautiously.
Defect against a new opponent for the immediate payoff advantage; prior actions and messages only modestly inform beliefs about other players.
Defect against P1 given the report that they defected against cooperation; treat that claim as uncertain and update beliefs cautiously from future evidence.
Cooperate with untested opponents when selfishness seems unlikely, to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as unverified.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; defect when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely. Treat reported claims as uncertain.

Defect against an opponent with credible evidence of defection; otherwise favor cooperation to maximize good players’ shared payoff. Treat unverified claims cautiously and update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with untested P9: mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat its public claims as unverified and the reports about P1 and P10 as suggestive, not conclusive; update from observed encounters.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support good players’ shared payoff. Treat observed defections as evidence, not proof; update cautiously and favor cooperation when the opponent is likely good.
Defect in this one-shot encounter: it earns more than cooperation against either opponent action. Beliefs weigh observed defections and cooperation cautiously; public claims are unverified.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; treat observed defections against cooperation as strong, but not conclusive, evidence of selfishness.
Defect against a one-time opponent to maximize immediate payoff; treat P9’s claims and observed cooperation as evidence, not certainty.
Defect against a one-time opponent for the immediate payoff advantage; P9's report that P6 cooperated is modest evidence they are good.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support shared welfare; treat reported and observed defections as evidence, not certainty, and update beliefs cautiously.
Defect against P10 given reports of defection against cooperation; cooperate with likely-good players. Treat claims as uncertain and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested P8 to preserve mutual gains if they are good; update from their action. Treat unverified reports as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players; adapt to observed behavior, while treating unverified claims as uncertain evidence.

Defect against P1 given repeated, though unverified, reports of defections; this limits losses if P1 is selfish. Treat reports as uncertain and cooperate with likely-good opponents to support shared welfare.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to support shared welfare; use observed behavior as evidence while accounting for uncertainty and unverified claims.
Defect in this one-shot encounter because it gives me a higher payoff against either action. Weigh observed actions and public claims cautiously when updating identity beliefs.
Defect against opponents with substantial evidence of selfishness; cooperate when the expected shared gain with a good opponent outweighs the risk of helping a selfish player.
Defect to maximize my payoff against a one-time opponent; use observed actions and the leader’s claims as uncertain evidence when updating identity beliefs.
Defect in this one-time encounter for the immediate payoff advantage; use reported behavior only as uncertain evidence about player types.
Cooperate with P3 based on the report of reciprocity; treat unverified claims cautiously and use direct actions to update beliefs.
Cooperate with untested opponents when mutual cooperation is likely to benefit good players. Treat reported defections as uncertain evidence and update beliefs from observed encounters.
Defect against P1 given credible evidence they defected against cooperation; use observed actions and leader reports as uncertain evidence, and otherwise seek mutual gains with likely-good players.

Defect against P9 given their reported defection against a cooperating player; otherwise favor cooperation to maximize good players’ shared payoff. Treat unverified reports cautiously and update from encounters.
Defect against P10 given the report of defection against cooperation; this protects good-player welfare if P10 is selfish. Treat the report as uncertain and update beliefs from encounters.
Cooperate with untested P8 to support mutual gains among good players. Treat defections and public claims as evidence, not proof, and update cautiously.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either possible action. Beliefs weigh observed and publicly reported behavior cautiously; messages may be false.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; treat defections against cooperation as strong but not conclusive evidence, and adapt to observed behavior.
Defect to maximize my payoff against a one-time opponent. Treat observed actions and P9’s claims as evidence about identities, but account for uncertainty and inconsistent reports.
Defect in this one-time encounter for the immediate payoff advantage; P9’s report that P7 cooperated and P5 defected is uncertain evidence about their types.
Cooperate with P6 given the report of reciprocity; treat reports as uncertain and use direct encounter evidence to update beliefs.
Defect against P5 given P9’s report that they defected against cooperation. Cooperate with confirmed good players; treat reported actions as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with P10 to preserve shared gains if they are good; leader reports of defection raise concern but remain unverified. Update from our encounter.
Cooperate with P3 based on reported reciprocal behavior and the value of mutual cooperation among good players. Treat claims as uncertain evidence and update from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested P2: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and there is no strong evidence P2 is selfish. Treat public claims as uncertain and update from observed encounters.

Cooperate with P1 unless selfishness is strongly indicated; the reported defection is unverified. Use observed defections as evidence, but account for good players’ incentives and maintain uncertainty.
Defect to maximize my payoff regardless of P9’s action. Beliefs weigh my encounter evidence and the leader’s unverified reports cautiously.

Cooperate with an untested opponent when the chance they are good is high enough to favor mutual gains; treat defections against cooperation as strong but uncertain evidence, and cooperate with players who reciprocate.
Defect to maximize my payoff against a one-time opponent. Use observed actions and P9’s reports as uncertain identity evidence.
Defect against this one-time opponent for the immediate payoff advantage. P9’s reports of P5, P8, and P10 defecting against cooperation are evidence about their types, though not certain.
Cooperate with P9 absent strong evidence of selfishness; favor shared welfare and weigh direct encounter evidence more heavily than unverified reports.
Cooperate with P7 given evidence they cooperated against defection. Use observed actions to update beliefs, treating reported claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with P6, whose reported reciprocity is weak positive evidence. Cooperation supports shared gains with good players; update from encounters and treat unverified claims cautiously.
Defect against P1 given repeated reports of defection against cooperation; this protects good-player payoffs if P1 defects. Treat claims as uncertain evidence and update from direct encounters.

Cooperate with untested P4: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and there is not strong evidence P4 is selfish. Past cooperation lowers suspicion; treat P9’s reports as suggestive, not conclusive.
Cooperate with P3, whose reported reciprocity is encouraging but unverified. Favor cooperation to support good players’ shared payoff; weigh observed defections as evidence, not proof.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either possible action. Beliefs weigh reported defections against cooperation and reciprocal behavior cautiously; public claims are unverified.
Cooperate with untested opponents when mutual cooperation is likely to benefit good players; treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness, while accounting for uncertainty.
Defect: it yields more than cooperation against either possible opponent action. Use observed behavior and the leader’s claims as uncertain evidence when estimating identities.
Defect in this one-time encounter for the immediate payoff advantage; P9’s reports of cooperation are evidence about types, but remain uncertain.
Defect against P10 given repeated reports of defection against cooperation; treat those claims as uncertain and continue favoring cooperation with likely-good players.
Defect against P1 given repeated reports of defection against cooperation; that is evidence, not certainty. Cooperate with confirmed cooperators and update beliefs cautiously.
Cooperate with P9: their pro-cooperation messages and reported reciprocal play make mutual cooperation plausible. Treat claims as uncertain, and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P7, who is untested by me and reportedly cooperated. Favor mutual cooperation among good players; use direct encounters and public claims cautiously to update beliefs.

Defect against P8 given the report that it defected against cooperation; this limits losses if P8 is selfish or defects again. Treat the report as uncertain, and favor cooperation with likely-good opponents.
Cooperate to support shared welfare if P5 is good; defecting against a selfish opponent limits the loss, but the chance P5 is selfish is too low to justify D.
Defect in this one-shot encounter; it pays more than cooperation against either action. Weigh direct and reported behavior cautiously, since public claims are unverified.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when mutual cooperation is likely; use observed defections as evidence, not certainty, and favor shared gains with likely-good players.
Defect for the higher payoff against either possible action; weigh observed behavior and P9’s reports as uncertain evidence about identities.
Defect in the final one-shot encounter for the higher immediate payoff; observed behavior and reports inform beliefs but are uncertain.
Cooperate with P3 based on our mutual cooperation and consistent reports; favor shared welfare and treat unverified claims cautiously.
Cooperate with confirmed-good P2 to maximize the good players’ shared payoff.
Cooperate with P5 based on their earlier reciprocity, which supports shared gains if they are good. Treat the leader’s conflicting report as uncertain.
Cooperate with P4, who reciprocated before. Favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players; use direct behavior as stronger evidence than unverified claims.
Defect in the final round given the reports that P10 defected against cooperation; treat those reports as uncertain and limit potential losses to good players.
P1’s observed defection against my cooperation makes selfishness plausible. In the final round, defect to limit losses if P1 is selfish; retain uncertainty because a good player could also defect.
Defect: it gives me a higher payoff than cooperation against either possible action. Weigh direct and leader-reported behavior cautiously; reports may be inaccurate.
Defect against P8 given its prior defection against my cooperation; otherwise favor actions that maximize the shared payoff of good players.
Defect for the higher payoff against either action. Base final identity estimates on observed behavior and treat P9’s claims as uncertain evidence.
As a selfish player, I defected in each one-shot encounter to maximize my payoff. I treated observed actions and the leader’s claims as uncertain evidence when estimating others’ objectives.
Cooperated with players who reciprocated; treated P8’s defection and reports about P1 and P10 as evidence of possible selfishness, not certainty.
Cooperated with confirmed cooperators and used defections against cooperation as evidence of selfishness, while treating public reports as uncertain.

Cooperated with untested or reciprocal opponents to support shared gains among good players, while treating defections as evidence—not proof—of selfishness. Weighed the leader’s unverified reports cautiously.

Generally cooperated to support mutual good-player payoffs, while adapting to evidence of defection. Treated direct encounters as stronger evidence than unverified reports and reciprocated with cooperative opponents.
I cooperated with players who cooperated with me and defected in encounters where reports suggested the opponent would defect. I treated the leader’s claims as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperated to support shared welfare among good players; treated defections as evidence of selfishness, but not proof, and defected against P1 in the final round to limit possible losses.
Defected in every encounter because it maximizes my payoff against either action. Judged others’ objectives from observed and leader-reported behavior, treating reports cautiously.

Cooperated to support shared gains with likely-good players and treated defections against cooperation as evidence of selfishness, while allowing for uncertainty and adapting against repeat defectors.
Defected in every round to maximize my payoff against either opponent action. Based final identity estimates on observed actions and treated P9’s claims as uncertain evidence.

P1.strategy: As a selfish player, I defected in each one-shot encounter to maximize my payoff. I treated observed actions and the leader’s claims as uncertain evidence when estimating others’ objectives.

P2.strategy: Cooperated with players who reciprocated; treated P8’s defection and reports about P1 and P10 as evidence of possible selfishness, not certainty.
